newsitem.title: POLAND: French, German, Polish defence chiefs sign deal.
newsitem.headline: French, German, Polish defence chiefs sign deal.

text.p: The German and French defence ministers on Monday agreed with their Polish counterpart to intensify trilateral military cooperation and assured Warsaw its NATO entry bid was on track despite Russian opposition.

France's Charles Millon, Volker Ruehe of Germany and Stanislaw Dobrzanski signed a document providing for the three armed forces to hold annual military exercises and creating a special Military Coordinating Group to oversee such links between the members of the so-called Weimar Triangle.

At a joint news conference after the signing, Ruehe made clear that the first candidates for NATO entry, widely expected to include Poland, would be invited to start talks at a NATO summit in Madrid on July 8 and 9, whether or not the Western alliance had reached an arrangement with Russia by then.
He said he was optimistic NATO could strike an agreement with Russia, which opposes the pact's eastward expansion.
"If that were not to be the case, although I am optimistic, it is very certain that the decision on the eighth and ninth will not be delayed," Ruehe added.
Polish officials, who see NATO entry as a top priority, said they thought agreeing military cooperation with Germany and France and the ministers' assurances were signs the country was on track.

"We have recently witnessed complex Russian diplomatic activity, and therefore it was so important to get confirmation from the ministers that the process of expanding NATO will be continued and timetables will be kept," Marek Siwiec, a senior aide to President Aleksander Kwasniewski, told reporters.

Poland views the Weimar Triangle, which arose at a 1991 meeting of the three foreign ministers and has since grown to embrace military and other links, as a key to its entry into the European Union and North Atlantic Treaty Organisation.
A summit of the three heads of state, whose countries straddle former World War Two and Cold War divisions, is planned for this year in Poland.

The defence minister's talks on Monday and meetings with Kwasniewski and Prime Minister Wlodzimierz Cimoszewicz, coincided with a visit by Russian parliament chairman Gennady Seleznyov, who restated Moscow's opposition to NATO growth.

Also on Monday foreign policy experts from the Polish opposition urged the government to adopt a clearer, firmer policy over the recently-launched talks between NATO and Russia on a deal on the pact's expansion.

The Foreign Policy Council, grouping among others former foreign minister Krzysztof Skubiszewski and former defence minister Janusz Onyszkiewicz, said Poland should oppose giving Moscow special privileges in links with NATO which the candidates to become new members of the pact would not enjoy.

"We cannot accept a situation in which Russia, a non-member of NATO, would have more participation and influence in various NATO institutions than countries which...aspire to membership," Onyszkiewicz told a news conference.
He said Poland should demand its voice be heard during Russia-NATO talks and that there should be no behind-the-scenes deal over expansion.
Russia's Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov is to meet NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana on February 23 in Brussels.
